title: Profit, Loss & Discount
summary: The highest-yield arithmetic block in Tier 1. CP–SP basics, successive discounts, the marked-price chain and dishonest-dealer cases appear in nearly every shift; Tier 2 layers on trade chains and price-shift comparisons. Everything reduces to multiplier chips.

subtopics.title: Profit, Loss and CP–SP Basics
subtopics.concept:
Profit and loss are **always calculated on the cost price (CP)** unless stated otherwise.

$$\text{Profit} = SP - CP, \qquad \text{Loss} = CP - SP$$
$$\text{Profit\%} = \frac{\text{Profit}}{CP} \times 100, \qquad SP = CP\left(\frac{100 \pm x}{100}\right)$$

**Multiplier chips:** profit of 20% → SP = 1.2 × CP; loss of 15% → SP = 0.85 × CP. Percentages as fractions are faster: 12.5% = $\frac{1}{8}$, 16⅔% = $\frac{1}{6}$, 8⅓% = $\frac{1}{12}$.

To recover CP from SP at x% profit: $CP = \frac{100 \cdot SP}{100 + x}$ — divide by the chip, don't take x% of SP.

tricks.title: Fraction ⇄ percentage swap
tricks.body: Convert the profit % to a fraction; SP/CP becomes a clean ratio.

example.q: A trader sells a cycle for ₹1,020 that cost him ₹850. Find the profit per cent.

tricks.title: Divide by the chip to get CP
tricks.body: SP given with a profit/loss %: undo the multiplier.

example.q: A machine is sold for ₹624 at a loss of 4%. Its cost price is:

tricks.title: Two prices, same % — scale linearly
tricks.body: If the same article at another CP/SP keeps the same profit %, everything scales by the same factor.

example.q: By selling 15 pens a man recovers the cost of 12 pens. His gain per cent is:

mistakes: Calculating profit % on SP instead of CP (a ₹20 profit on SP 120 is NOT 16⅔% gain).
Recovering CP as $SP - x\% \text{ of } SP$ — that's the SP-based error again.
Mixing up profit and loss chips (0.9 is a 10% loss, not a 10% discount on profit).
Ignoring that 'gain of 25%' and 'marked 25% up' refer to different bases (CP vs MP).

subtopics.title: Successive Changes & Equivalent Single Change
subtopics.concept:
Two percentage changes applied one after another do **not** simply add — the second acts on the already-changed value.

$$\text{Net change} = a + b + \frac{ab}{100} \quad (\text{use } -b \text{ for a decrease})$$

- Same change x twice: increase $2x + \frac{x^2}{100}$; decrease $2x - \frac{x^2}{100}$.
- Two discounts of $d_1, d_2$: equivalent single discount $= d_1 + d_2 - \frac{d_1 d_2}{100}$.

**Chip method:** multiply $(1 \pm a/100)(1 \pm b/100)$ — this never fails, even for three changes, and reverses cleanly.

tricks.title: Multiply the chips
tricks.body: Chips work for any mix of increases and decreases, in any order.

example.q: A price is increased by 20% and then the new price is decreased by 10%. Net change?

tricks.title: The d₁ + d₂ − d₁d₂/100 formula
tricks.body: Two discounts collapse in one line.

example.q: Find the single discount equivalent to two successive discounts of 20% and 10%.

tricks.title: Work backwards through chips
tricks.body: For 'find the second change given the net', divide the net chip by the first chip.

example.q: After a rise of 25% a value was changed again and ended 15% up overall. Find the second change.

mistakes: Adding successive discounts directly (20% + 10% = 30% is wrong; the answer is 28%).
For a profit then a loss, using +ab/100 where the sign must be negative.
Applying the second discount on the original marked price instead of the reduced price.
Assuming the order of changes matters — chip multiplication is commutative.

subtopics.title: Marked Price, Discount and the CP–MP–SP Chain
subtopics.concept:
The full chain: trader **marks up** CP to MP, then allows a **discount** on MP to reach SP.

$$\text{Discount} = MP - SP, \qquad \text{Discount\% is always on MP}$$
$$MP = CP \times \frac{100 + g}{100 - d}, \qquad SP = MP\left(\frac{100 - d}{100}\right)$$

Multi-level trade (manufacturer → wholesaler → retailer) chains the same way: multiply each markup factor $\left(1 + \frac{x}{100}\right)$.

If a discount of d% still leaves a gain of g%, the markup on CP must be $\frac{(100+g)}{(100-d)} - 1$ times CP.

tricks.title: Build the MP/CP ratio
tricks.body: Gain g% and discount d% together fix MP as a multiple of CP.

example.q: After allowing a discount of 10% on the marked price a trader still gains 20%. The marked price is how much per cent above the cost price?

tricks.title: Markup chip then discount chip
tricks.body: One chip for the markup, one for the discount.

example.q: An article costing ₹1,000 is marked 25% above cost and sold at a 15% discount. Find the profit per cent.

tricks.title: Trade-chain multiplication
tricks.body: Each middleman's markup is one chip.

example.q: A manufacturer sells to a wholesaler at 20% profit, the wholesaler to a retailer at 25% profit, and the retailer to a customer at 10% profit. If the customer pays ₹3,300, the manufacturing cost is:

mistakes: Taking the discount on CP instead of MP.
Forgetting that profit % is still on CP while discount % is on MP — the two bases differ.
In trade chains, adding the markups (20 + 25 + 10 = 55%) instead of multiplying chips (65%).
Reading 'marked 25% above cost' as MP = 125 when CP = 100 — right — but then applying discount % to CP.

subtopics.title: Dishonest Dealer, False Weights & Claims
subtopics.concept:
The dealer cheats on the **quantity**, not the price. Compare true goods against paid goods.

**Sells at CP with false weight:** using w g instead of W g gives
$$\text{gain\%} = \frac{W - w}{w} \times 100$$

**Claims a loss but cheats on weight:** claims L% loss but gives c% less weight ⇒ true multiplier $= \frac{100 - L}{100 - c}$.

**Cheats both ways** — takes b% extra while buying and gives s% less while selling: multiplier $= \frac{100 + b}{100 - s}$.

Setup a per-1000 g table: what he pays for, what he actually gets, what he actually gives.

tricks.title: The W−w over w rule
tricks.body: Loss to the customer is measured against what the dealer actually gave.

example.q: A shopkeeper sells rice at cost price but uses a weight of 900 g for 1 kg. Find his gain per cent.

tricks.title: Claimed loss can still be a gain
tricks.body: Compare the money per TRUE gram, not per claimed gram.

example.q: A merchant claims to sell at a 10% loss but gives only 800 g per kg. Find his actual gain or loss.
example.solution: Per true kg he receives $0.90$ and pays $0.80$: gain $= \frac{0.9 - 0.8}{0.8} = 12.5\%$.

tricks.title: Both-ends multiplier
tricks.body: Multiply the buy-side gain chip by the sell-side chip.

example.q: A dishonest dealer takes 10% more goods than he pays for and sells 10% less than the true weight. His gain per cent is:

mistakes: Using $\frac{W-w}{W}$ instead of $\frac{W-w}{w}$ (the base is what the buyer actually received).
Believing a '10% loss' claim without checking the weight.
In both-ends cheating, adding the two percentages instead of multiplying chips.
Mixing up which side the cheat favours — dealer gains when buying AND when selling.

subtopics.title: Same Selling Price: One Profit, One Loss
subtopics.concept:
Two articles sold at the **same price**, one at x% profit and the other at x% loss, always end in a **net loss**:

$$\text{Net loss\%} = \left(\frac{x}{10}\right)^2 = \frac{x^2}{100}$$

Why: total $CP = \frac{S}{1 + x/100} + \frac{S}{1 - x/100} > 2S$. The loss is small but never zero.

If asked for amounts, reconstruct each CP by dividing the common SP by its chip.

tricks.title: The x²/100 reflex
tricks.body: Same SP, opposite equal % → straight to the loss formula.

example.q: Two mobiles are sold for ₹1,200 each — one at a 25% profit and the other at a 25% loss. Find the overall per cent loss.

tricks.title: Reconstruct both CPs, then total
tricks.body: Divide the common SP by each chip.

example.q: Two articles are sold for ₹1,680 each; one at 20% profit, the other at 20% loss. Find the net loss in rupees.

mistakes: Concluding 'no profit no loss' because the percentages cancel — the base amounts differ, so there is always a loss.
Using $\frac{x^2}{100}$ when the profit and loss percentages are unequal — reconstruct CPs instead.
Reporting the loss per cent as the loss amount (₹140 is not 140%).
Dividing SP by the wrong chip (profit article: divide by 1 + x/100, loss article: by 1 − x/100).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: CP and SP given (or one derivable in one step); find the profit or loss per cent.
pyqPatterns.approach: Find the difference, divide by CP, multiply by 100. Fraction equivalents (1/8 = 12.5%) skip the arithmetic.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One of CP/SP given with the profit or loss % — find the other.
pyqPatterns.approach: Apply or undo the chip: SP = CP × (1 ± x/100). 'Had it been sold for ₹k more/less…' ⇒ the k spans the difference of two percentages of CP.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Two successive discounts of 20% and 10%', or a rise followed by a fall.
pyqPatterns.approach: Chips multiply; equivalent single discount $= d_1 + d_2 - \frac{d_1d_2}{100}$. Never add discounts.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Marked x% above cost, discount y% allowed, find gain % (or work back to MP).
pyqPatterns.approach: $\frac{MP}{CP} = \frac{100+g}{100-d}$ fixes any one of MP/CP, gain, discount from the other two.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: False weights, short measure, or a claimed loss with cheating on quantity.
pyqPatterns.approach: $\text{gain\%} = \frac{W - w}{w} \times 100$; for claims, compare money per TRUE unit. Cheating at both ends multiplies chips.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Same SP, one profit one loss
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two items sold at the same price with equal ±x% — the net result.
pyqPatterns.approach: Net loss% $= \frac{x^2}{100}$; if amounts are asked, reconstruct both CPs.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Manufacturer → wholesaler → retailer, each adding a profit %.
pyqPatterns.approach: Multiply the markup chips end to end; divide to walk backwards to the base cost.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Cost of goods sold / goods-based cases
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Sells at CP the quantity equal to the cost of 20 units', 'recover the cost of 12 pens by selling 15'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Set up units: profit in units ÷ cost in units = gain fraction. Translate words into a fraction of CP.

solvedExamples.solution:
$SP = 1.20\,CP$ and $SP = 0.90\,MP$ ⇒ $MP = \frac{1.2}{0.9}CP = \frac{4}{3}CP$.
So MP is 33⅓% above CP. (E.g. CP ₹600 → MP ₹800, SP ₹720.)

solvedExamples.q: A dishonest shopkeeper sells sugar at the cost price but uses a weight of 900 grams in place of 1 kg. His gain per cent is:
solvedExamples.solution: Gain is on the 900 g he actually gave: $\frac{1000 - 900}{900} \times 100 = 11\frac{1}{9}\%$.

A man sells a scooter at a loss of 5%. Had he sold it for ₹960 more, he would have gained 15%. The cost price of the scooter is:
practice.solution:
The swing from $-5\%$ to $+15\%$ spans $20\%$ of CP.
$0.20 \times CP = 960$ ⇒ $CP = 4800$, i.e. ₹4,800.
practice.shortcut: Difference of the two percentages = 20% of CP ⇒ 960/0.2 = 4,800.

practice.shortcut: Trade-chain chips multiply to 33/20 ⇒ divide 3,300 by 1.65.

practice.q: A man sells an article at a profit of 12.5%. Had he sold it for ₹51.80 less, he would have incurred a loss of 6%. The cost price of the article is:
practice.solution:
The price difference spans $12.5\% - (-6\%) = 18.5\%$ of CP.
$0.185 \times CP = 51.80$ ⇒ $CP = 280$, i.e. ₹280.
